senses: A type of concert hammered dulcimer used primarily in the music of Central and Eastern Europe.
ety: From Hungarian cimbalom. Doublet of cymbal.

senses: A male harvester; any harvester (person who works to gather in the crops at harvest time).
An order of terrestrial, non-venomous arachnids with often very long legs: Opiliones; any individual of this order.
ety: From harvest + -man. (sense 2): There are various hypotheses and folk etymologies for why the arachnids are called harvestmen, but the most likely explanation is the shape of their legs, which resemble sickles or scythes. senses: In the culture of the Indian subcontinent, an effeminate man who takes on a passive or female gender role in same-sex relationships.
One who cuts hay for animal fodder.
The community of all followers of the Buddha; the ecclesia in which the devout take refuge; those who have "entered the stream" towards nirvana; one of the Three Jewels of Buddhism.
The Buddhist congregation including laypersons and the "religious" (renunciate monks and nuns who have taken vows).
ety: Transliteration of Sanskrit सङ्घ (saṅgha, “heap, multitude, crowd”).

senses: The act or process of notarizing.
Something notarized.
Having (or producing) excessively high blood sugar.
To absorb and process as if by metabolism.
Any of several similar plants
Agastache foeniculum, blue giant hyssop.
ety: Via Latin hȳsōpum, from Ancient Greek ὕσσωπος (hússōpos), of Semitic origin.

senses: A kind of lunchbox or food container.
Food prepared for domestic pet animals.
A deep type of dish or pan, typically used for casseroles and made out of pottery.
A pâté baked in such a dish and served cold.
ety: Borrowed from French terrine (“a clay dish; that which is cooked in the dish”). Doublet of tureen.

senses: A shoe protector (metal stud or plate affixed to the sole or heel of a shoe to prevent excessive wear).
ety: Genericized trademark of Blakey's Segs, a British brand of shoe protector, named after John Blakey, who invented them in 1880.

senses: A large herbivorous sauropod dinosaur, Brachiosaurus altithorax, which lived during the Late Jurassic in North America.
ety: Borrowed from taxonomic name Brachiosaurus, from brachio- + -saurus; literally “arm lizard”, relating to the great length of its forelegs compared to its hindlegs.

senses: A type of nationalism which defines the nation in terms of a shared ethnicity.
examples: It risks triteness to note that during the past two decades ethnonationalism has been an extremely consequential force throughout the first, second, and third worlds.
As central Party control weakened, independence demands grew in other republike, inspired in part by local ethnonationalisms and fear of living in a Yugoslavia dominated by Serbian ethnonationalists.
Since 1863 Polish 'National Democrats' like Roman Dmowski had abandoned the idea of a multinational commonwealth for a more 'modem' Polish ethnonationalism.

senses: An abortion.
An aborted fetus, especially one aborted in early pregnancy.
ety: Borrowed from New Latin abortus (“miscarriage”). Doublet of abort.

senses: Undoing or dissolution of conversion.
The loss of faith in a given religion and return to a previously held religion or non-religion (typically atheism, agnosticism, or rationalism).
A traditional type of formal hairstyle for unmarried women in Japan, whereby the hair is gathered together and fastened to the top of the head.
An ornament of Greek origin, or Greek-style, especially a fretwork
A vessel with a perforated bottom for making coffee without grounds.
examples: The sleeves are wide; the revers, or deep cuffs, being formed by a grecque similar to that of the skirt.

senses: A black-clad person who enters the stage to rearrange the set, unremarked by the actors
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 後見(こうけん) (kōken, “a staff in noh and kabuki”).
examples: McAllister uses the Japanese device of the koken for changing scenes, distributing props, and creating furniture.

senses: A type of pasta, with rolled edges.
ety: From Italian cavatelli (literally “little hollows”), plural diminutive of cavato (“hollow”) (+ -ello (diminutive), pluralized).
examples: Little Owl’s cavatelli with salty bacon, fava beans and a bracing, sweet tomato broth benefits from the lush, mouth-filling quality of the ricotta crumbled on top.

senses: Any book containing two or more epics.
A lengthy, revered narrative poem, ordinarily concerning a serious subject containing details of heroic deeds and events significant to a culture or nation.
Not fractionated
The valuable timber of these trees.
ety: From Burmese ပိတောက် (pi.tauk).
examples: In the dusty workroom her artificially red ponytail glowed like padauk, one of the exotic veneers she uses in her work.

senses: A mixture of metals resembling brass.
A mixture of different sorts of grain, such as wheat and rye.
ety: From Middle English missellane, misceline, miscelin, meslin, from Old English mæstling, mæsling, mæslen. See also miscellane.

senses: A machine that extrudes material through shaped dies
An expert in gemology.
examples: Sundararajan was among the observers, along with several archeologists and gemologists.

senses: The fused head and thorax of spiders and crustaceans.
A CSS3 layout model that allows elements on a web page to be arranged in certain ways within a one-dimensional container.
An HTML element that uses this model.
examples: Internet Explorer 9 does not support flexbox.
The contents of a flexbox can be positioned in any direction, can have their order swapped dynamically, and can auto-adjust their sizes and positions based on available space.

There's still quite a bit of tumult in the standards recommendations and implementations for flexboxes, but IE10 and Windows 8 has a good, solid implementation of this extremely helpful layout technique.

senses: Lying or floating above a denser fluid, or above a solid sediment or precipitate (which has been separated by crystallisation, centrifugation etc.).
A musical instrument, endemic to the Top End of Australia, consisting of a long hollowed-out log which, when blown into, produces a low, deep mesmerising drone with sweeping rhythms.
ety: Likely onomatopoeic in reference to the sound made by the instrument, or the words spoken into the instrument to play it. The earliest known description of the instrument was in 1829 by Captain Collet Barker, in which it was described as making the sound didoggerry whoan. In 2002, Lonergan proposed that the term could derive from Irish dúdaire dubh (“black hummer”) or Scottish Gaelic dùdaire dùth (“native piper”), though the latter seems to be coincidental, since there is no corroborating evidence and the terms would refer to the player (rather than the instrument itself).

senses: A mathematician who specializes in algebra.
Ochre-colored.
One who carries anything away, or the vessel in which things are carried away.
One who avoids, shuns, or escapes.
examples: Perhaps the most fundamental discussion we ought to have is how for years we allowed routine tax avoiders to be classed as "philanthropists" because of their other activities.

senses: A type of island consisting of a ribbon reef that nearly or entirely surrounds a lagoon and supports, in most cases, one to many islets on the reef platform.
ety: Borrowed from Portuguese atol, from Dhivehi އަތޮޅު (atoḷu), possibly from Prakrit *𑀲𑀁𑀢𑀻𑀞 (*saṃtīṭha), from Sanskrit सम्- (sam-) + तीर्थ (tīrtha) “level ford”. The traditional etymology from Persian آبتل (âb-tal, “water-hillock”) is unlikely.

senses: A collection of manuscripts; an anthology.
One who studies some branch of learning, especially one ending in -ology; a specialist.
examples: First was the increasing number of ologists. While they were far from dominant, their voices were heard throughout the agency, and what they said caused many of the foresters to think.
I was talking with my ologist this week and he asked if I felt like I was in a fog.
Ologist physicians dominate America's healthcare system. An ologist might take care only of your bones, your skin, or your liver.

senses: The hunting of wild animals.
Game animals.
ety: From Middle English venerie, borrowed from Middle French venerie, from Old French venerie (“hunting”), derived from vener, from Latin vēnor (“to hunt”).
